sourceBindings.text: Low or high pH suggests a direction, not a product dose. Use the measured result, intended crop, reserve acidity or buffering, and the soil-test recommendation to explain when lime, elemental sulfur or organic inputs might help and when more evidence is needed.
Explain when an acidic crop field may need calcitic or dolomitic liming, and when elemental sulfur could be considered for a high-pH field, with the chemistry and time limits.

Explain why two soils at the same pH can need different amendment rates, and list the crop target, appropriate soil-test or buffer information, soil type, material quality and site constraints needed before calculating an amount.
Interpret the source's A/B/C model values and the soybean pH 5.2 case without treating model values as measured observations or compost as a universal pH treatment.

sourceBindings.text: The classroom model labels A near 5.5 and asks which direction would help corn, but the actual field sample and lime requirement are not yet known.
If a reliable test confirms low pH for the intended corn system, liming is the standard direction; sulfur would lower pH further.
Request the crop-specific target and lime requirement or reserve-acidity result, plus material quality and magnesium status before choosing calcitic versus dolomitic material and any rate.
If this is only the prepared classroom model, do not turn its 5.5 label into a field application order.
Choose a direction from the problem; choose an amount from the soil test and product.

sourceBindings.text: A learner sees the classroom model's high-pH Sample C and says to add one bag of sulfur today so potatoes can be planted tomorrow.
Sulfur can acidify only after microbial oxidation; a one-day guaranteed pH change is not supported.
Investigate crop needs, carbonate content and buffering, water and site conditions; a strongly calcareous field may resist whole-field acidification.
Use a tested, feasible plan and follow-up measurements, or reconsider crop/site choice. No bag count follows from pH 7.9 alone.
High pH is a question to investigate before recommending sulfur.

sourceBindings.text: A sandy field and a clay-rich field both test pH 5.2 for the same crop, and a learner proposes the same lime rate for both.
The pH reading describes active acidity; the clay-rich soil may hold more reserve acidity and resist change more strongly.
Ask for the appropriate buffer/lime-requirement result and product neutralizing power for each field; similar pH does not mean identical rate.
Recheck the crop target and application conditions before offering a field recommendation.
pH tells you the direction; buffering helps determine the amount.

sourceBindings.text: Last year's soybean was stunted and yellow; a reliable test now shows pH 5.2 and a preliminary report suggests low available P.
Acidic conditions could contribute to P availability and aluminum-related root stress, but symptoms also have other causes.
Confirm representative soil and crop-context tests, including a calibrated P test and lime requirement. Interpret the report for the next crop.
Consider liming if recommended and address P separately with a locally supported source/rate. The classroom's bone-meal/rock-phosphate option is not a universal automatic prescription.
Do not treat one symptom or a multiple-choice option as a complete fertilizer plan.

sourceBindings.text: Sort four case cards into 'likely raise pH', 'investigate possible lowering', 'soil health input rather than pH cure' and 'insufficient evidence'. Place A 5.5/corn, B 6.8/unspecified crop, C 7.9/potato and soybean 5.2; then request the missing crop, carbonate, buffer/lime-requirement, P and product data before releasing any rate. A comparison card asks which of sandy and clay-rich soils at the same pH is more buffered. After each choice explain why and receive specific feedback.

This is a reasoning step. If you are using real sample A/B/C readings, follow the supervised measurement instructions and separate practical record from S2-06 or S2-07. This step asks you to justify a possible amendment and identify missing information; it does not authorize applying lime, sulfur or manure to a field.

Use real A/B/C measurements from S2-06 or S2-07, with a private pretested key. Rotate tester, recorder and chart analyst roles between samples; verify kit quantities using its instructions, record the spread of readings, explain disagreement, and clean the station before discussion. The trainer may guide a group explanation, but this K-only step is assessed on each learner's reasoning, not a new hands-on endorsement.

sourceBindings.text: amendment
A material added to soil for a stated purpose, selected and dosed from crop and soil evidence.
calcitic lime
A liming material chiefly supplying calcium carbonate; it does not inherently supply magnesium.
dolomitic lime
A calcium-magnesium carbonate liming material that can supply magnesium when needed.
reserve acidity
Acidity held on soil exchange sites in addition to the active acidity represented by a pH reading.
buffering capacity
The soil's resistance to pH change; often influenced by clay, organic matter and carbonates.
calcareous soil
Soil containing free calcium carbonate, which can strongly resist attempts to acidify the whole field.
